task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper reported feature for general readers. Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of March 6, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: Dr. Hana Park, a neuroimaging methodologist at Westfield University, published a paper in January 2025 identifying a systematic error in the motion artifact correction algorithm used by a widely distributed neuroimaging tool, MotiCalc-3.

The error causes the algorithm to overcorrect for head movement in datasets with high variability between scan sessions, systematically biasing estimates of between-group differences in brain activation.
Dr. Park's analysis found that the bias direction favors finding differences between groups where none exist, rather than masking real ones.
MotiCalc-3 is used in an estimated 2,800 published fMRI studies; the affected version (MotiCalc 3.4 through 3.7) was the default tool in neuroimaging pipelines between 2017 and 2022.
Dr. Park said: "I found this because I was trying to replicate a result in my own lab and couldn't. When I traced why, I found it in the algorithm. Then I found it everywhere."

The field does not have a mechanism for systematically flagging papers that used affected software; the journal where the original MotiCalc-3 paper was published has issued an editor's note linking to Dr. Park's correction.

Clare Finch, a second-year graduate student at Westfield, worked with Dr. Park to write the reanalysis scripts; she said the work took 11 months and required re-running data from seven studies with author cooperation.
Finch said: "Seven studies cooperated. They were able to share data. Most papers from that era didn't archive their raw data. We couldn't test those, even if we wanted to."

Of the seven studies reanalyzed with corrected software, three maintained their original findings; two showed reduced effect sizes that fell below statistical significance; two showed different patterns of activation.

Dr. Park said she does not know how representative the seven studies are of the broader 2,800; the cooperating authors were self-selected and may not reflect the distribution of potential error severity.

The developers of MotiCalc-3, software consortium NeuroTools Collaborative, acknowledged the error in a February 2025 statement and released a corrected version; they said they had not been aware of the issue before Dr. Park's paper.

A statement from NeuroTools said the error was introduced in a 2017 update that was peer-reviewed as part of a methods paper but that the specific motion correction pathway was not directly tested in that review.
Dr. Park said she had no criticism of NeuroTools' response: "They fixed it quickly and transparently. The problem is the papers that used the broken version are still in the literature."

An independent neuroimager, Dr. Thomas Brennan of Pacific University, said the field had already known about methodological problems in motion correction since the 2016 software bug discovery; Dr. Park's finding adds to a pattern rather than being isolated.

Dr. Brennan said: "We have a cumulative knowledge problem. Individual corrections are published. The affected papers stay in databases. The field's self-correction mechanism is slow relative to how fast results propagate through the media and into policy."

Finch said she is aware that her work will be cited in debates about the reliability of neuroimaging and is careful about how she characterizes the scope: "It's not that fMRI doesn't work. It's that a specific tool had a specific bug. Those are different claims."

Dr. Park said she has been contacted by researchers in clinical settings who used affected studies as evidence for treatment protocols; she does not know how many, and declined to characterize the clinical impact without further analysis.

The journal Neuroscience Methods Review has published an editorial calling for a voluntary reanalysis registry where authors can report whether their studies used affected versions of MotiCalc; as of March 2025, 34 authors have registered.
Dr. Park said her lab will continue the reanalysis project: they hope to test an additional 20 cooperating studies in 2025 and will publish all results regardless of outcome.
Finch said: "We're not trying to tear down a field. We're trying to make it accurate. Those are the same thing, eventually."

forbidden_additions: a clinical harm directly attributed to the software error
a retraction count for affected papers
an effect size or activation finding not derived from the seven analyzed studies
